questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_111-->When selecting the right design elements in producing your message, list the seven tips discussed to make your message more attractive and contemporary.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Reflect a modern appearance to help busy readers get your message. 2. Emphasize main parts of your message by balancing text with graphics. 3. Use white space to show organization and provide visual contrast for your readers. 4. Use headings, which are short phases that summarize a section of the document, to emphasize key content. 5. Improve readability through margins and layout. 6. Choose easy-to-read typefaces but be sure to limit the number of type faces to no more than two on a page. 7. questiontext.text: Tamara is the editor of her company's newsletter. For years, the newsletter has used a drab style that is not very reader-friendly. How can Tamara change this into a style that is easier to read using typeface choices and margins? Explain Tamara's options in terms of typefaces and margins and explain which she should choose to achieve this.

generalfeedback.text:
Typeface: Typeface influences the tone of your message, making it look authoritative or friendly, businesslike or casual, classic or modern. Tamara should take care to choose a typeface that is appropriate for business use without being too formal. Serif typefaces are commonly used for body text. They can look busy and cluttered when set in large sizes for headings or other display treatments. Sans serif typefaces, in contrast, lack these serifs. The visual simplicity of sans serif typefaces such as Helvetica and Arial makes them ideal for the larger sizes used in headlines. Sans serif faces can be difficult to read in long blocks of text, however, unless they are formatted with generous amounts of leading, or spacing between lines. Tamara can use a serif typeface for the body text and a suitable sans serif for headings and subheadings. Tamara should take care not to use more than two typefaces for the newsletter, as it may look too cluttered or amateurish.


Margins: Margins define the space around text and between text columns. In addition to their width, the look and feel of margins are influenced by the way you arrange lines of text, which can be set 1. Justified (which means they are flush, or aligned vertically, on both the left and the right), 2. Flush left with a ragged-right margin, 3. Flush right with a ragged-left margin, or 4. Centred. Though it accommodates more words than other alignments, justified type needs to be used with care. First, it creates a denser look because the uniform line lengths decrease the amount of white space along the right margin. Second, it produces a more formal look that isn't appropriate for all situations. Third, unless it is formatted with skill and attention, justified type can be more difficult to read because it can produce large gaps between words and excessive hyphenation at the ends of lines. Because most business communicators don't have that time or skill, it's best to avoid justified type in most business documents. In contrast to justified type, flush-left, ragged-right type creates a more open appearance on the page, producing a less formal and more contemporary look. Spacing between words is consistent, and only long words that fall at the ends of lines are hyphenated. Centred type is rarely used for text paragraphs but is commonly used for headings and subheadings. Flush-right, ragged-left type is rarely used in business documents. As it is a business publication, Tamara can use a left-aligned format for it is easier to achieve and gives a contemporary look that is easy to read.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_113-->Explain the importance and process of proofreading. Why does it matter and what should you look for?

generalfeedback.text: This essay should mention that proofreading is important because errors make a document harder to read and understand and detract from the writer's credibility. When proofreading, you should look at every word and punctuation mark, as well as the overall format and design of the document. This includes a wide range of elements, such as page layout, margins, consistency, headings, type size, typeface, grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling, columns, and graphics.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_114-->Discuss the seven tips for proofreading. What is an effective process?

generalfeedback.text: This essay should address the following seven points: 1. Read a document several times when proofreading; focus on different aspects each time. 2. Use tactics to avoid the errors and typos your brain has been trained to ignore. These include reading the page backward, reading aloud, and reading each word or sentence alone. 3. Have others proofread for you. 4. Try to wait a day or two after writing the document before proofreading it. 5. Avoid proofreading large amounts of text in one sitting. 6. Focus carefully on what you are doing. 7. Take your time; don't rush proofreading.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_115-->List three of the four methods for preventing perceptual tricks.

generalfeedback.text: 1. Read the document backwards-from bottom to top. 2. Place your finger under each word and read it silently. 3. Make a slit in a sheet of paper that reveals only one line at a time. 4. Read the document out loud.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_012-->Explain how the design techniques work together to create an effective message.

generalfeedback.text:
The five design techniques are: 1. Balance all visual elements; 2. Strive for simplicity in design; 3. Be consistent throughout a message; 4. Pay attention to design details; 5. Use the best technology available.
This essay should discuss the importance of paying attention to all of these elements to help readers quickly read and understand a business document. Well-designed documents balance text, graphics, and white space. They do not look cluttered, and they do not overwhelm readers. Writers need to be consistent in their use of margins, headings, type size, and typeface; all design details should be carefully considered. Finally, technology can greatly help with the process of designing a document that looks professional and is easy to read.

questiontext.text: You often have several options for distribution of a message. What are the factors you should consider when making your choice? List four.

generalfeedback.text:
• Cost. Cost isn't a concern for most messages, but for multiple copies of lengthy reports, or multimedia productions, it might be. Be sure to consider the nonverbal message you send regarding cost. Overnight delivery of a printed report could seem responsive in one instance and wasteful in another, for example.
  • Convenience. Make sure your audience can conveniently access the material you send. For instance, sending large files may be fine on a fast office network, but receiving them can be a major headache for recipients on slower wireless networks.
  • Time. How soon does the message need to reach the audience? Don't waste money on overnight delivery if the recipient won't read a report for a week.
  • Security and privacy. The convenience offered by digital communication needs to be weighed against security and privacy concerns. For sensitive messages, your company will likely restrict both the people who can receive the messages and the means you can use to distribute them. In addition, most computer users are wary of opening attachments, particularly word-processing files. As an alternative, convert your documents to PDF files using Adobe Acrobat or an equivalent product.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_127-->What is telepathic communication? Provide one example.

generalfeedback.text:
Mental telepathy-sending and receiving messages purely through the power of the mind-has long been a staple of science fiction and the province of psychics. However, some rudimentary experiments in technology-enabled telepathy show at least a hint of promise that telepathy could add an intriguing element to business communication in the future.
Using existing medical technologies for sensing and stimulating brain activity, scientists at the University of Washington demonstrated a simple video game in which one user's thoughts controlled a second user's physical motions. When the first user saw something on their screen and made a decision about how to react (without actually moving their hand), that brain activity was detected and transmitted to a second user. Using essentially the reverse technology, the decision the first user made would stimulate the brain of the second user and cause this second user to move their hand to implement the decision via a game controller. In a separate test, an international team of researchers showed it was possible to send simple verbal messages using a similar concept of encoding and decoding.

questiontext.text: List four factors that influence the distribution of a message. Explain how each factor has an influence on the choice of medium.

generalfeedback.text:
Cost: Cost isn't a concern for most messages, but for multiple copies of lengthy reports or multimedia productions, it could be. Weigh the cost and the benefits before deciding on a medium.

Convenience: Make sure your audience can conveniently access the material you send. For instance, sending huge files may be fine on a fast office network, but receiving such files can be a major headache for remote colleagues trying to download them over slower wireless networks.

Time: You have to consider how soon the message needs to reach the audience. Don't waste money on overnight delivery if the recipient won't read a report for a week.

Security and privacy: The convenience offered by electronic communication needs to be weighed against security and privacy concerns. For the most sensitive messages, your company will probably restrict both the people who can receive the messages and the means you can use to distribute them. In addition, most computer users are wary of opening attachments these days. Instead of sending word processor files, which are vulnerable to macro viruses and other risks, you can convert your documents to PDF files using Adobe Acrobat or an equivalent product.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_013-->List the three main tasks involved in completing a business message.

generalfeedback.text: Revising your message is the first step. This involves rewriting and editing for clarity and conciseness. The next step is producing your message. This involves selecting an appropriate and effective design and using computers to improve your message. Finally, the third step is proofreading your message to improve its professional image and yours.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_062-->Explain the importance of revising for clarity.

generalfeedback.text: This essay should discuss the problems that can result from an unclear document. Readers may not understand key points, writers may not accomplish their purpose, and time may be wasted trying to determine the writer's intent.

questiontext.text:
Correct the parallelism problems in the following paragraph.
In order to graduate on time, he will have to take courses in finance, marketing, and how to do account management. But in order to pass them, he will have to study hard, go to class, and will probably have to be working fewer hours at his campus job.

generalfeedback.text: To graduate on time, he will have to take courses in finance, marketing, and account management. But to pass them, he will have to study hard, go to class, and work fewer hours at his campus job.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_064-->List and describe the nine techniques for revising for clarity.

generalfeedback.text: The nine techniques are: 1. Break up overly long sentences-don't connect too many clauses with and. 2. Rewrite hedging sentences-avoid using may or seems. 3. Impose parallelism-use the same grammatical pattern to express two or more similar ideas. 4. Correct dangling modifiers-delete phrases with no connection to the subject of the sentence or those that are too closely placed to the wrong noun or verb. 5. Reword long noun sequences-avoid stringing many nouns together as modifiers. 6. Replace camouflaged verbs-watch for verbs that have been turned into nouns. 7. Clarify sentence structure-keep the subject and predicate of a sentence as close together as possible. 8. Clarify awkward references-avoid words and phrases that cause readers to jump from point to point. 9. Moderate your enthusiasm-don't overuse adjectives and adverbs to sound falsely positive.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_065-->Discuss the importance of making a document more concise.

generalfeedback.text: This essay should discuss the preference of many business executives for shorter documents. Also, time is important in the business world and shorter documents will save time. Additionally, people are more likely to read shorter documents-long blocks of text will discourage most readers. Finally, many documents are much longer than they need to be. The extra words are a detriment to clear and quick understanding.

questiontext.text: <!--RsQ_066-->List and explain the four techniques for making documents more concise.

generalfeedback.text: The four techniques are: 1. Delete unnecessary words and phrases-frequently you can say something more efficiently with one word than you can with a longer phrase. 2. Shorten long words and phrases-short words are generally more vivid and easier to read than long ones are. 3. Eliminate redundancies-avoid word combinations that say the same thing. 4. Rewrite "it is/there are" starters-you can usually shorten sentences that start with these phrases.

questiontext.text: Describe the techniques you should use when designing messages for mobile devices.

generalfeedback.text:
- Think in small chunks. Remember that mobile users consume information one screen at a time, so try to divide your message into independent, easy-to-consume bites. If readers have to scroll through a dozen screens to piece together your message, they might miss key points or just give up entirely.
- Make generous use of white space. White space is always helpful, but it's critical on small screens because readers are trying to get the point of every message as quickly as possible. Keep your paragraphs short (four to six lines) and separate them with blank lines so the reader's eyes can easily jump from one point to the next.
- Format simply. Avoid anything that is likely to get in the way of fast, easy reading, including busy typefaces, complex graphics, and complicated layouts.
- Consider horizontal and vertical layouts. Most phones and tablets can automatically rotate their screen content from horizontal to vertical as the user rotates the device. A layout that doesn't work well with the narrow vertical perspective might be acceptable at the wider horizontal perspective.
